claims.statement: Malachi prophesied after Nehemiah's first governorship (after 433 BC), rather than shortly before his reforms.
claims.reasoning: Keil (after Vitringa) dates Malachi after Nehemiah's first term because its abuses match Neh 13; Guzik agrees broadly. Smith prefers the years just before the reforms: a governor accepts gifts, which Nehemiah refused (Neh 5:14–18), and no recent covenant is mentioned; he sets the outer limits at about 510 and 312 BC. No external evidence decides it.

claims.statement: Edom had suffered a recent devastation by Malachi's time, probably the Nabataean displacement from its heartland (before 312 BC).
claims.reasoning: Smith infers a recent blow to Edom from 1:3–4 and notes that southern Judah was called Idumaea by 312 BC, the Nabataeans having displaced the Edomites (citing Diodorus 19.94–100 after Hieronymus of Cardia); the date of the displacement is unknown. Diodorus was not read directly in this unit.
limitations: Secondary report of Diodorus; Edomite archaeology not consulted.

evidence.finding: After the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes; Mal 2:11 ~ Neh 13:23; Mal 3:8–10 ~ Neh 13:10–14.
Best taken as preparing the way for Nehemiah's reforms.
At the time of Nehemiah or immediately afterwards.
The Nabataean overrunning of Edom probably the disaster meant; Idumaea by 312 BC.

research_gaps: Diodorus 19.94–100 and Edomite/Nabataean archaeology not read.
